children: In response to the question “Where you slep las nigh?,” one of the crew heading for Burke’s pub at the end of Oxen of the Sun says, “Timothy of the battered naggin.” The phrase refers to Sir Timothy O'Brien, an early 19th century innkeeper whose establishment was in the Liberties near St. Patrick’s cathedral. He supposedly acquired the nickname The Knight of the Battered Naggin by serving drinks in battered metal cups that enabled him to deprive customers of their full measure.

children: Annotating for etymology.
“Tally ho” was a cry raised during a fox-hunt when the quarry was sighted.
It dates from around 1772, and is probably derived from the French taïaut, a cry used to excite hounds when hunting deer.

Taïaut may have originated in the second half of the 13th century by the concatenation of a two-word war-cry: taille haut. “Taille” is the cutting edge of a sword and “haut” means high or ‘raised up’. So the original meaning might be something close to “Swords up!”.
